display_title: Why Your Gym Routine Isn't Working
display_title_he: למה שגרת האימונים שלך לא עובדת
short_summary: Experts reveal common fitness mistakes, from over-relying on cardio to ignoring nutrition and recovery, and explain how to achieve sustainable results.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Going nowhere fast? Personal trainers on why you aren’t seeing results in the gym

paragraphs: Many individuals embark on a new fitness journey with immense enthusiasm, often triggered by a fresh start or a desire for change, only to abandon their efforts shortly thereafter. Personal trainers emphasize that the secret to long-term success lies in consistency rather than fleeting intensity. Instead of launching into an unsustainable five-day-a-week schedule that life inevitably disrupts, it is far more effective to devise a realistic plan. Elizabeth Davies, author of 'Training for Your Old Lady Body', suggests starting with two weekly strength sessions. If you maintain this, you can always add a third, building on a foundation that is actually sustainable.

A prevalent misconception is the belief that one must constantly rotate exercises to 'keep the body guessing'. Experts like Nick Finney, who has trained celebrities such as Jennifer Lopez, argue that this approach hinders progress. Frequent changes make it impossible to measure improvement. Instead, he advocates for 'progressive overload'—the systematic increase of weight or repetitions. By mastering a specific movement, you provide your body the necessary stimulus to adapt and grow stronger. Furthermore, while cardiovascular exercise is vital for heart health, exclusive focus on it neglects fast-twitch muscle fibers, which are essential for preventing frailty and falls as we age. Osteopath David Vaux recommends combining movement with resistance training two or three times weekly.

When training for muscle growth, one must work 'close to failure'—the point where another good repetition is impossible. Many confuse the burning sensation of high-rep sets with true muscle failure, yet this burn is often just a buildup of metabolites. Nutrition remains the most significant factor in physical change. Many gym-goers overestimate the calories burned during a workout; a grueling session might only burn the equivalent of one and a half apples. If your goal is weight loss, you must maintain a calorie deficit, whereas muscle building requires a surplus and roughly 2g of protein per kilo of body weight. Additionally, people frequently overlook hidden calories in juices, smoothies, and alcohol.

Finally, reject the 'go hard or go home' mentality, which frequently leads to injuries like tendinitis. Fitness is a long-term investment, not a punishment. Avoid comparing yourself to social media influencers, whose results may be skewed by years of training, image editing, or performance-enhancing drugs. Instead, be intentional with your time. Put your phone away, plan your sets, and allow for proper recovery. By focusing on sustainable, consistent effort, you can transform your gym time into a meaningful investment in your future health.

facts.fact: Personal trainers advise against constantly changing workout routines, recommending 'progressive overload' instead.
Focusing exclusively on cardio neglects fast-twitch muscle fibers, which are essential for mobility as we age.
Training close to failure is necessary for muscle growth, and discomfort from high-rep sets is not the same as true muscle failure.
Nutrition is the most significant factor in fitness progress, as exercise alone rarely burns enough calories to offset poor dietary habits.
Consistency and recovery are more important than high-intensity training, which can lead to injury.
